::: {.resource-intro}
**The essential idea:** Peer review is collaborative inquiry into whether a piece works for its purpose and audience. Revision rethinks meaning and structure; copyediting improves expression after the larger decisions are sound.
:::

## Core practices

### Begin with the writer’s goal

Ask what the writer wants readers to understand and what kind of feedback is most useful now.

### Prioritize substantive issues

Comment first on focus, evidence, organization, audience, and argument; address sentence-level details later.

### Document choices

Convert comments into a short revision plan and record why you accepted, adapted, or declined key suggestions.

## A simple workflow

Read once without marking. Summarize the main message in your own words. On a second pass, note one strength, one significant question, and one specific revision suggestion tied to a location in the draft.

## In context

::: {.callout-example}
A reviewer notices that a restoration proposal introduces its recommendation before showing evidence. Instead of “reorganize,” they identify the relevant paragraphs and suggest an evidence-first sequence.
:::

## Keep in mind

Feedback is information, not an instruction to obey every suggestion. The writer remains responsible for the final piece.
